summary:
Micah prophesied "in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah" (1:1) — roughly the second half of the 700s BC, the years in which Isaiah also prophesied (Isaiah 1:1). He came from Moresheth, a small town in the foothills southwest of Jerusalem, and he addresses both capitals: Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, and Jerusalem, capital of Judah. Assyria destroyed Samaria in 722 BC, within Micah's lifetime, and invaded Judah under Hezekiah in 701 BC.

The book moves in three rounds, each opening with a call to "hear" (1:2; 3:1; 6:1) and each passing from judgment to hope. The judgment targets the powerful: those who "covet fields and seize them" (2:2), rulers who "tear the skin from my people" (3:2), and a capital where "leaders judge for a bribe, her priests teach for a price, and her prophets practice divination for money" (3:11), while claiming, "Is not the LORD among us? No disaster can come upon us" (3:11). Micah's verdict: "Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble" (3:12). A century later, elders quoted that sentence to defend Jeremiah when his temple sermon put his life on trial (Jeremiah 26:18) — a rare case of one prophet quoted by name inside another prophetic book.

In the hope sections, the nations stream to "the mountain of the house of the LORD" and "beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks" (4:1–3); nearly the same lines appear in Isaiah 2:2–4, and who drew on whom, or whether both used a shared source, is not known. Micah 5:2 names the coming ruler's birthplace: "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel" — the verse the chief priests and scribes cited when Herod asked where the Christ would be born (Matthew 2:6). Chapter 6 stages a courtroom: God brings "a case against His people" (6:2) and distills His requirement into one sentence: "He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?" (6:8).

The name Micah is a short form of Micaiah, "Who is like the LORD?" The closing lines echo it: "Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance — who does not retain His anger forever, because He delights in loving devotion?" (7:18). The "remnant" is the surviving part of the people God preserves, one of the book's repeated words (2:12; 4:7; 5:7–8). Its final promise: "You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea" (7:19).
